newsitem.title: BELGIUM: North-South divisions widen in scandal-hit Belgium.
newsitem.headline: North-South divisions widen in scandal-hit Belgium.

text.p: Belgium, briefly united in its grief and anger over the paedophile murders of young girls, has quickly slid back into bickering between its French and Dutch-speaking halves.
Rivalry between the two communities is nothing new, but this time the bile is much more bitter.

The scandal of kidnapped, sexually abused and murdered children gave rise to public demand for a radical change in the way Belgium works. But political analysts say that impulse is in danger of being hijacked by a handful of politicians on opposite sides of the country's linguistic divide.

"There are a few politicians who are trying to manipulate public opinion to their own ends," Helmut Gauss, Professor of Political Science at Ghent University, said in an interview. "There is a lot of dirty party politics."

The arrest of child rapist Marc Dutroux in August and the discovery of the bodies of four young girls at first brought Belgians together. More than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in October in a so-called White March of sympathy and protest.

But the mood of unity has evaporated and there has been a growing feeling that something is rotten in Wallonia, the French-speaking southern half of Belgium. Not only were the murdered girls found there, but several Walloon politicians have been the subject of sex or bribery allegations.

The French-speaking Socialist Party has been beset by allegations of sexual misconduct against one minister, charges of links to a murder against another former minister and bribery against several senior officials.
"The White March was an expression of mass sentiment. The arguments that have come up since are at the level of the political elite," Gauss said.
"There are a few people who are trying to point the finger of blame at Wallonia for all the problems."

Divisions between the country's two halves are exacerbated by economics. Wallonia, historically an industrial powerhouse but now more of a wasteland, relies heavily on financial help from the state which is generated mostly by Dutch-speaking Flanders.
French-speaking politicians resent the dominance of the Flemish.
Philippe Busquin, president of the scandal-hit Francophone Socialists, hit out recently at what he called "new Flemish imperialism."
"Wallonia is not yet a Flemish protectorate," Robert Collignon, President of the Walloon regional government, said.

Gauss said there was growing discontent among Flemish businessmen at the amount their region contributed to Walloon coffers, but it was unclear whether this was a real upsurge in separatist sentiment or simply jockeying for position.
Luc Van Den Brande, President of the Flanders regional government, never known to miss an opportunity to promote his region and belittle his southern cousins, has also joined the fray.
While carefully avoiding calling for a separate Flemish state, he said earlier this week that a core of European regions should form the heart of Europe.
It should include southern Britain, northern France, Flanders, the Netherlands and western Germany, he said, specifically excluding Wallonia.

According to Gauss, Van Den Brande is stealing some of the clothes of strongly nationalistic Flemish parties like the Vlaams Blok and Volksunie in a bid to win over their voters to his Christian Democratic party.

Gauss said it was vital to remember that while national elections are not due until the end of 1999, they could take place at any time after the European Union decides early next year which countries will be the first to join its single currency, the euro.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene will fight to keep his four-party coalition government together at least until his burning ambition of getting Belgium into the first wave of euro members has been achieved.
But that means there could be an election in about a year -- so this is prime time to begin quiet campaigning.
"Dehaene will fight for as much time as possible. At the moment the greens and the nationalistic parties are in the ascendant, but voters have short memories and time is votes," Gauss said.

"The mainstream parties are reinventing and renewing themselves. If they can delay the election into 1999 that process will be completed, the justice reforms will be in place and some heads will have rolled in the Dutroux affair."
